utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber was informed that both parties have preliminaries. I think the Defence wanted to move into private session for the preliminary. Mr. Lukic, we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, first I was going to tender the letter of the witness's son which Mr. Lukic spent quite a bit of time with yesterday. It's 65 ter 18349. But when I discussed this with Mr. Lukic, he expressed that it was his intention to tender it, so if he does that now I'll have no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections. Of course, we wanted to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You want to tender it. Let's then deal with that first of all. 65 ter 18349 would receive what number, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D53, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D53 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next matter is the Prosecution at this time would tender 65 ter 28432. This is the chart containing Mr. Selak's observations of eight documents. And Your Honours, the 65 ter numbers those documents is contained on the chart itself. Your Honour, this past Tuesday, at transcript page 2963, the Chamber expressed concern over this chart and what the Chamber termed as creativity of the Prosecution which might lead to a situation that the Chamber wanted to avoid. Although the Chamber was not explicit about its concerns, I understood the Chamber to be referring to its previously expressed concern of large numbers of unnecessary or marginally relevant documents. I would like to address the Chamber's concern in the context of this exhibit. There were 34 documents the Prosecution considered using with this witness. An examination of the previous testimonies of Mr. Selak reveals additional exhibits which would meet the legal test of relevance. The Prosecution selected eight of the most directly relevant ones for admission through a proposal that the Defence accepted as a fair way to deal with the exhibits and I think was clearly a more efficient way to adduce the evidence of military documents which largely speak for themselves. Document 1 is a JNA 5th Corps report dated the 14th of May, 1992, a week of importance in this trial. The document sets forth the state of the command and control structures in what would soon become the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, if would you allow me one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, the Chamber mainly expressed some concerns in a more general way about a possible development of the procedure. The Chamber is not seeking at this moment a justification for each of these documents. Unless the Defence would object to them, of course, then we'd like to hear further explanation. But at this moment the Chamber is - and you have understood that well - is concerned that -- and we didn't say that you had flooded the Chamber. I think even at the time when it happened we did not know even how many documents would be on the chart. I'm not quite certain about the time -- moment in time. But at this moment, also knowing now the number involved, we are not assisted by a full explanation at this moment. If it comes in the near future to similar situations, it might be that we would like to receive further justification.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If now is not a convenient moment for the Prosecution to make these submissions, I accept that. I would make a request to be able to address the concerns of the Chamber. It is a matter of some importance to the Prosecution and in -- so at a time when the Chamber is prepared to hear these submissions, I would ask that we do it, and I recognise there is a witness here waiting to be called. But if it doesn't assist the Chamber at this time, I will not insist upon making my submission at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The submissions you made until now, for this instance, Mr. Groome, satisfies the Chamber. And if you want to address the matter in a more general way in the near future, you will have an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Or if at any time the Chamber has this concern, I'm prepared to answer it at any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's then --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So Your Honour, that just leaves us with the matter of the tendering of that chart and the underlying exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, which was announced to be done at the end of the examination of the witness. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Our understanding of this chart is only to give the opportunity to the witness to confirm authenticity or not and it's not, in our understanding, something that should lead to -- to tender these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that was clear on from the beginning. I think that we said that we would decide on the admission of the chart and the documents at the end of the testimony. I'll check that in the transcript, but I would be surprised if I said anything else. And apart from that, the witness, of course, gave in the chart his comments as well. I mean, what's the use of hearing the comments of the witness if the underlying document is not accessible, is not in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In our -- our position is that he would then be shown the documents and tell us about the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He has reviewed the documents and the instructions in the chart clearly says what he's -- what he is expected to do. That's at the top, do this, do that, do that, do that, and then write down this or write down that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you see the chart, document number 1, I'm not going to take much of your time, it says: I have not seen this document. I'm unsure of its authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear. And that's why the box authentic or non-authentic is not ticked, as a matter of fact, whereas it is for others. But the witness here says, I cannot say anything about the authenticity of this document. He didn't tick the box and he explained why.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would that document be tendered then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that is tendered by Mr. Groome, and whether we will admit it or not depends on our decision and what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you look at that box, you would realise that the witness also did not initial it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what I meant by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But the others that he --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Others have initials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Others are initialed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

And if you want to challenge the admission on the basis of authenticity, of course, you can do so. And the Chamber would then have to rely on your submissions, Prosecution submissions, and any other indications of authenticity, because the witness cannot help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, first, the chart, in the understanding now, Mr. Lukic, and I'll check whether I said admission -- about admission. Any objections against the chart?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections against the chart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, if I could seek your assistance because I don't have the chart here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a spare -- I have two spare copies so I can either --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you take them --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I could spare one or I can go one by one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you take them one by one, if you mention the number we'll hear from -- and briefly say what it is, and then we'll hear from Mr. Lukic whether there are any objections. The first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is 65 ter 16015. It's an order of the 5th Corps issued on the 14th May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic. If you want to say -- if you're not prepared, then we'll leave it for later this morning so that can you make up your mind, because apparently you were not expecting the underlying documents to be tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, I would kindly ask Your Honours to give me some time and prepare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, at this moment, we'll not deal with the underlying exhibits and only deal with the chart itself where there were no objections against admission. Mr. Registrar, the chart would receive number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P259, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P259 is admitted into evidence. And we'll deal with the underlying documents at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any other preliminary matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The Prosecution is prepared to call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the Chamber has another matter which it would like to raise. Which is the following. And, Mr. Lukic, please listen carefully, and, Mr. Mladic, also listen very carefully to what I'm going to say. The Chamber has now, at five occasions - that means in relation to five witnesses - received complaints about the behaviour of Mr. Mladic. Most recently about his behaviour of yesterday where we identified three instances, one of them including an observation made by Mr. Mladic that the witness lied. In relation to five witnesses, verbally or otherwise commenting, reacting to testimony. This has led the Chamber to establish a new regime. The accused will not be allowed any further to consult with counsel in court. The accused may pass a little note, if needed, but silently to counsel. Consultations can take place during breaks. The accused is not allowed to speak in court. Any violation will result in the removal of the accused from court. This new regime has been established because, on the one hand, the Chamber cannot understand the words the accused speaks, audible for others; and, second, because the accused has shown that he repeatedly interfered in an unacceptable way with the witnesses, which the Chamber does not allow. Mr. Lukic, is this new regime clear to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Although I have to stress one thing. Mr. Mladic writes very slowly and sometimes when we get its note it's too late or we have to readdress the same issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's all the consequence of what happened. I referred to five witnesses where we received such claims. Some of them, of course, we have dealt with already in the past. It's a pity. Then you will be able only a few minutes after that, or after the next break, to respond to that. That is -- the Chamber would not have spontaneously would have imposed this new regime. It is because of our experience with the behaviour of the accused in court that we felt that we could not do otherwise in order to protect the witnesses. Mr. Groome, is the Prosecution ready to call its -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Prosecution calls Sulejman Crncalo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Traldi. We'll wait until the witness arrives in court. No protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. And while the witness is being called into the courtroom, Your Honour, I will reiterate from our filing that Mr. Crncalo's evidence does overlap with certain adjudicated facts. We have reviewed Mr. Crncalo's 92 ter material and made redactions on the basis of facts 1679 and 1683. We have also redacted paragraphs of Mr. Crncalo's statement which we deemed not directly relevant to the adjudication of this indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the redactions do not meet any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Ivetic will cross this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ivetic, if there is anything in those redacted paragraphs, of course, this would not prevent you from addressing any matter which is found in those paragraphs. Although the Chamber is not aware of that content at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I understand that, and I believe that the Prosecution has the right to prepare their statements how they want. If there's material I will address it. No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Crncalo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Crncalo. Mr. Crncalo, you'll first be examined by Mr. Traldi. Mr. Traldi is counsel for the Prosecution, and you'll find him to your right. Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. How are you feeling this morning?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And if at any time you aren't, please don't hesitate to ask the Chamber and ask us to take a break.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, sir, then could I ask you to please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: My name is Sulejman Crncalo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And what is your ethnicity, sir?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: My ethnicity is Bosniak, Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, do you remember providing a statement to the ICTY on 1 November 2009?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd ask the Court Officer to please display 65 ter 28427 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, Mr. Crncalo, now that the document is on the screen before us, can I ask that we go to the last page of the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I note they're both in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I have a B/C/S hard copy with me, Your Honour. And I'd note that now the left side of the screen reflects the B/C/S version. I apologise. It's the next-to-last page that I'm looking for?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the English, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, sir, if you look on the right side of your screen in the bottom corner, I'd ask if you recognise the signature that you see there.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I do, it's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And have you had an opportunity to read and review this statement in preparation for your appearance here today?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I'd ask the Court Officer to please display 65 ter 28436 on our screens. It is a chart of clarifications to the statement which was disclosed to the Defence this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, have you had an opportunity to review this document in preparation for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And does it accurately set out clarifications to your statement which you made during the course of preparation for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If I were today to ask you questions about the material in your statement, would you provide the same information, in substance, subject to the clarifications you have provided in this document?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I would give the same statement, the same clarifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And now that you have taken the solemn declaration, do you affirm, Mr. Crncalo, that you provided the information in both these documents truthfully?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I provided truthful information. I have no other information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 28427 and 28436 into evidence pursuant to Rule 92 ter, as public exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Traldi, has the Chamber been provided with the clarifications? Previous -- prior to coming into court today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I believe they're in e-court, Your Honour, but I'm afraid we haven't provided you a hard copy. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is a 92 ter witness. That means that the Chamber should, prior to coming to court, be informed about any changes in relation to the 92 ter statement the Chamber has looked at before and has considered before coming to court. Therefore, I would like to instruct the Prosecution that if any such clarifications, again not about the viva voce witness, then you can present it viva voce in court. But if it relates to any 92 ter statement, the Chamber should be provided with such a clarification, even if not filed then at least brought to our attention in other ways. Having said this, Mr. Registrar, the numbers for these two documents would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 28427 shall assigned Exhibit P260. And 65 ter document number 28436 shall be assigned Exhibit P261. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P260 and P261 are admitted into evidence. And just for your understanding, Mr. Traldi, do you expect the Chamber to go without knowing about 65 ter numbers through the whole of the e-court in the morning to find out whether there's anything new? That would be a lack of understanding of what the Chamber is reasonably expected to do. Especially since we have no 65 -- we shouldn't do it anyhow, but certainly we could not possibly do it without even having 65 ter numbers. Please proceed. Mr. Crncalo, this had nothing to do with you, but Mr. Traldi will now start his further examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and the clarification chart was identified on the exhibit list we provided to the Chamber and the Defence, but in future we'll provide you with a hard copy as well. And that e-mail was sent on 25 September at 5.24 p.m., for your records. At this time, Your Honour, I would also tender the associated exhibits mentioned in our 92 ter filing for this witness. That's 65 ter 03665, 03736, 11113, 11114, 11115, and 11116. As well as the table of concordance for this witness labelled with 65 ter 28363.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objections to these, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Registrar, could you assign numbers to them one by one.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 03665 shall be assigned Exhibit P262.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 03736 shall be assigned Exhibit P263.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 11113 shall be assigned Exhibit P264.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 11114 shall be assigned Exhibit P265.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 11115 shall be assigned Exhibit P266.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 11116 shall be assigned Exhibit P267.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And 65 ter number 28363 be assigned Exhibit P268.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Mr. Traldi, I'm still looking at ... could you provide us with a copy where you said it was mentioned on the list of exhibits, because we have the annex A to the motion at the time, and I have another list in my hands where I have difficulties to find the clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we'll print out the e-mail and the list at the break, if that's convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's convenient. And if I made a mistake, then, of course, I apologise for that. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Now that the requirements of Rule 92 ter have been satisfied, I will briefly summarise Mr. Crncalo's written evidence for the record. Mr. Crncalo is a Bosnian Muslim from Pale. He was part of a delegation which met with a member of the Bosnian Serb Presidency named Nikola Koljevic in the spring of 1992. Koljevic told the delegation that the Serbs did not want Muslims living in Pale. In June 1992, Radovan Karadzic gave a speech in front of the Dom Kulture in Pale. Mr. Crncalo heard Karadzic say that the best way to defend Serb houses was to attack Muslim houses. Soon afterwards, Mr. Crncalo and other Muslims were forcibly removed from Pale in convoys organised by the Serb authorities. Several Muslims who refused to leave the area were killed, and the three mosques in Pale were destroyed, as charged in Schedule D10 of the indictment. Mr. Crncalo and his family fled to besieged Sarajevo where they remained for the remainder of the war. There he lived in constant fear that he and his family would be killed. When Mr. Crncalo left home, he was never sure that he would return alive or that those he had left behind would be alive when he returned. On several occasions, he saw civilians killed by snipers. On 28 August 1995, Mr. Crncalo's wife went to the Markale market-place to shop for powdered milk. She didn't come home, so Mr. Crncalo went to search for her. On his way, he heard about the shelling of the market-place charged in Schedule G.18 of the indictment. When he got to Markale, his wife was not there. He looked at the hospital but didn't find his wife there either. He then went to the morgue, where he found his wife's body.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, now that we've reviewed your written evidence, I'm going to ask several questions to clarify or expand upon that evidence.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, you describe in your statement a meeting with Nikola Koljevic and what he said to you. I'm going to ask you only one focussed question about this meeting. When Koljevic spoke to you and the other Muslims in your delegation, what was your understanding as to whether he was speaking on behalf of Serb authorities in the area?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: We first went to see the chief of the municipality, asking for our safety to be guaranteed to continue living in Pale. He sent us to the police chief. We put the same question to the chief of police. He sent us back to the head of the municipality. And he said that he couldn't guarantee our safety, and this is what the chief of the municipality, the head of the municipality told us. We then asked both of them to bring in someone --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I'm sorry to interrupt, but may I ask you again to move forward from when you spoke with the police chief and the chief of the municipality to when you spoke with Koljevic, directly, and ask you whether in your understanding Mr. Koljevic was speaking on behalf of the Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: He was speaking on behalf of the Serbian authorities at the time. And he told us that the Serbs did not want to live with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I'm going to move now to paragraph 59 of your statement, Exhibit P260. In the that paragraph, you say that your neighbour, Fehim Hrvo, was arrested and later killed. Do you know where he was imprisoned?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: He was imprisoned in an old facility -- in an old cinema, in fact, which was close to the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Do you know if there was ever an investigation into his death?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: No. An investigation was not conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Okay. And in paragraph 60 of your statement, P260, you say Izet Jasarevic, Alija Jusufovic, and Nasko Smajic were also killed. Was there ever an investigation into any of their deaths?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: No. An investigation was not launched into their deaths.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Next, Mr. Crncalo, I want to take you to paragraph 78 of P260. In that paragraph, you say that you saw Radovan Karadzic give a speech in Pale in June 1992. What first brought you out of your house that evening?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: My health is not very good, but I do smoke and in such stressful situations I started smoking even more. I didn't have any cigarettes so I went to buy some cigarettes. There was a little kiosk down by an old hotel. I went to the kiosk and there was some sort of a meeting by the Dom Kulture, the cultural centre. I know what it was about. I won't go into that. Radovan was giving a speech at that meeting, and he said, We have to attack all Muslim houses, wherever they may be. In this manner, you will be defending your own house, end of quote.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And are you sure of that word, sir, that he said "all" Muslim houses?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I'm now telling you what I heard him say. As to what he thought, I don't know. But I'm telling you what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So just so the Trial Chamber understands, sir, your answer is, yes, you are sure you heard him say that word?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I heard him, and I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: About how far away from Karadzic were you at the time?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, I would say I was about 15 metres away, give or take a metre. I can't say precisely. All I can do is assume that that was the distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And then, Mr. Crncalo, you describe in your statement being forced to leave Pale and arriving in Sarajevo. When you joined the convoy and other Muslims joined the convoy to leave Pale, did some Muslims remain in Pale?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, they did remain. Five families remained: The Mutapcici husband and wife; and Ramiz Kujovic and his wife Hasna; and then Muharem Kujovic remained; Ziba Kadic remained; and a mother and daughter, Alija Hodzas and Hajra.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You say in page 80 -- or, sorry, paragraph 80 of P260, you name some of these people and say they were killed. My question is: Of the Muslims you know who remained in Pale, did any of them survive the war?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: No one survived the war. I went to the burials of some of them after exhumations had been carried out, but I know that Ziba Kadic didn't survive. However, I don't know whether she died of natural causes or whether she was killed. I couldn't say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I'd ask the Court Officer now to please call P178, the municipalities map book, to the screen, and turn to page 33.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: While they do that, Mr. Crncalo, you singled out Ziba Kadic and said you couldn't be sure if she died of natural causes. Does that mean you are sure that the other people were killed?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes. Some of them were found in pieces in the municipality of Pale. That's what their son told me when he went to the exhumation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's addition: They were found in Gornji Bare.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, sir, you'll see a map now on your screen labelling the mosques in Pale. Based on your memory, does the map accurately reflect the position of those maps?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I'd suggest that we zoom in a little bit for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not necessary, I can see it. The sites at which the mosques were located are quite clearly and correctly marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you say in your statement, sir, that you heard that after you left the mosques in Pale were destroyed. You referred to the period between July and September 1992. Who controlled Pale at that time?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: At the time, Pale was under the control of the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And now I want to turn to your time in Sarajevo. In paragraphs 89 and 90 of Exhibit P260, you mention that you were near certain civilians who were hit by sniper fire. Did you see either of those shootings yourself?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes. I was personally present, and I saw the incident. The first person who died by the Hotel Bristol was wearing jeans and a jean jacket, and I didn't know there was a sniper firing there. He tried to cross the road and he was hit by a sniper. He only managed to move ahead a bit and fell down and there was a puddle of blood at his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And aside from these two incidents described in your statement, sir - on Brodska Street and at the Hotel Bristol - did you ever see anyone else hit by gun-fire in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes. I saw people being killed on television, but as for being present and seeing people being killed, well, yes, in Brodska Street and at the Hotel Bristol I did see such incidents. But all the streets were covered in blood, and I was continually stepping in that blood.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, finally, Mr. Crncalo, I have to ask you briefly about the morning of the 28th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: For the Chamber's and Defence's reference, this is discussed in Exhibit P260, starting at paragraph 94.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: First, sir, had you been to Markale market yourself during your time in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: When you went to the market, what kind of people would you usually see there?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, usually ordinary people who had nothing to live off. They'd go there to buy some food, if anyone was selling food there. So usually it was these very ordinary people, the most ordinary people who would be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Had you ever seen anyone there carrying a gun?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: There were no such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You say in paragraph 94 of your statement that you left home that morning to look for your wife after you heard a shell. Around what time was that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, my wife was supposed to return - that's what we had agreed on - about half past 10.00 or 11.00. When she did not turn up, I had to go to look for her.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And in paragraph 95 -- and, again, Mr. Crncalo, please don't hesitate to tell the Chamber if you need a break. In paragraph 95 --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I'll continue now. I went to look for her. Halfway there, others asked me where I was going. I said I was going to Markale. My wife left. She hasn't returned. They said a catastrophe happened over there. I said, What happened? They said a shell fell. I went up there. I'll never forget that image. It will never leave me. The street was covered in blood. There were about 30 there -- well, that's my assessment. But the part hit by the shell was covered in blood. There was a fence protecting pedestrians from the trams, and there were body parts or, rather, parts of clothing and a footwear on the fence, in the streets. There were body parts. The entire fence was covered in blood. I observed all of this and there were people looking on from side streets. They asked me, What are you doing? I said, I'm looking for my wife. There seemed to be wounded, people who were dead there. And they put them on -- in vehicles and took them to the hospital. I went to the hospital. I arrived at the hospital. There were lists that had already been compiled and they were on the door. I searched for my wife on the list. I couldn't find her name. Then someone turned up in a white overall and asked me whether I had had a look in the morgue. I said, No. They said, Go there. Maybe it was a doctor. I don't know. I arrived a room and I recognised her immediately. There was seven bodies there. My wife was the third body in that row. The bodies were the bodies of women. It's only human to cry, and I started crying. Three individuals appeared from another room and asked me, Have you recognised her? I said, Yes. Crncalo, Pasa. They noted this down. I went home then and told the children. So that's what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, this completes my examination. And looking at the clock, I'd suggest it might be an opportune moment for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Traldi. Mr. Crncalo, we'll take a break at this moment. Would you please follow the usher. We'd like to see you back in approximately 25 minutes from now. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we take that break, first of all, Mr. Traldi, there's no need to provide the e-mail. The e-mail was sent, as I see, by Ms. Stewart on the 25th of September at 5.24 p.m. in the afternoon. It was even clearly indicated that 65 ter 28436 has been added. Now, perhaps for a better understanding. Non-associated exhibits - and this is one - non-associated exhibits are exhibits that the Prosecution may use. Now, the Chamber usually does not start studying these documents. We then have the 65 ter number, so in that respect I was wrong when I said it's very difficult to do that without 65 ter numbers, but even with the 65 ter numbers the Chamber waits and sees whether the party - and that is equally true for Prosecution and for Defence - wish to use that document and wish to tender that document. That's different with associated exhibits which are considered to be an inherent part of the 92 ter statement. Now, a -- this document, clarification, directly relates to the 92 ter statement, which the Chamber has reviewed, because it was part of the motion, and, therefore, the Chamber rather would not find it on a list of non-associated exhibits you may use. But if it's clear that you want the statement to be corrected in accordance with such a document, then we should receive that document itself and not just the 65 ter number. Otherwise, the Chamber would have to start to select from your non-associated exhibits which one which we think most likely you would use or would not use, and that's really not how it should work. I take it that the Defence takes a similar position, and expects the Chamber to do the same, in relation to exhibits the Defence may use. We wait to look at it until you use it. Therefore, such clarification should need a different treatment. We take a break, and we resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I could briefly raise a matter. On the 25th of September, the Prosecution has inquired about changing the witness schedule in relation to the testimony of Witness RM081. I don't think that we have already received the position of the Defence. Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm trying to find RM081.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that the one that you said --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah. I can see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It was -- [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So in that week we have three witnesses; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No. The Prosecution sent an e-mail, and we did discuss it briefly in court. This is a person who was detained in the Vlahovac school in Rogatica, and our proposal was to have him available to testify Friday next week if there was hearing time available.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's fine with the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you are -- you may proceed as suggested, Mr. Groome. And there's another matter I would like to raise in this context but I will do that later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you are cross-examined, Mr. Crncalo, Judge Fluegge has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, I would like to put one question to you. At the beginning of the examination by Mr. Traldi, you were asked about a certain person, Nikola Koljevic. Can you help me, what position did this man held? Was he -- what -- what post did he held? Have you any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was the deputy prime minister of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That was all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Ivetic. You'll find Mr. Ivetic to your left. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of the -- of Mr. Mladic. Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, I would ask today that you focus your answers to be directly responsive to my questions and then we'll get through this as quickly as possible. Is that understood, sir?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And furthermore, I would ask that if something I say or ask is not clear to you, that you bring it to my attention. Is that okay, sir?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: While I do appreciate everything you have gone through, I need to get to the full truth of things together with you, if you will permit me. Is that agreed, sir?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In that case, I will begin, sir. First of all, just prior to the break, the Prosecution counsel asked you about various mosques in the municipality of Pale that you state had been destroyed. Insofar as you were gone from Pale municipality from July 1992 until the end of the war, would you agree with me that you do not have independent personal knowledge of how these mosques in Pale were damaged or destroyed?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I learned after the war that the mosques in Praca and Podvitez were mined. Explosives were set up. The one in Bogovici burnt down because it was mostly made of wood. The cemetery next to the Podvitez mosque was bulldosed so that no one would know any longer where each of the graves were.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You -- you have no information of when that was done and by whom it was done, do you, sir?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I was told that it was done by the Serb forces in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me move along to the section where you identified several individuals that stayed in Pale municipality after you left and for whom you said that they were deceased. I would like to focus for a moment on Ziba Kadic, whom you indicated that you were not sure of how she had become deceased --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, paragraph number?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. That would be -- that would be the testimony that -- that we just had before the break. I do not believe it is a separate -- I do apologise. It is a paragraph -- Ms. Kadic is not mentioned in the amalgamated statement. She has been omitted by the Office of the Prosecutor. She is mentioned in the last paragraph of the prior statement, but the paragraph in this statement, P260, is paragraph 80.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see. Do I --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Which is on page 14 in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Just for my understanding, you say it was about a person which was -- is not in the statement and also not in the testimony, is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: He testified to her. Her name is not in this statement. It is contained in a prior statement that the Office of the Prosecutor had of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the Chamber is not familiar with any prior statements. The Chamber is only familiar with this statement, so therefore I have to check. Is it anywhere on the transcript of today.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Immediately prior to the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, immediately. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And perhaps to make it easier for everyone, if we could pull up 1D285, which is a copy of the statement taken by the Office of the Prosecutor on 8 June 2001 with this witness. And if we can turn to page 8 in both versions in e-court. And while we wait for that, I can spend the time efficiently with the witness with the lead-in to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, am I correct that you -- since returning to Pale, you have been informed or advised that Ms. Ziba Kadic died after the war of natural causes?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Ziba did not see the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we ... could we have the right page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This does appear to be the right page, Your Honour, the eighth page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, first of all, if we look at the English version of the document that is before you, is that your signature depicted as one of the three signatures on this statement?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, if you could direct your attention to the last paragraph on that page. In this statement given to the Office of the Prosecutor, you identify Ms. Ziba Kadic as an individual who not only stayed behind in Pale but who also was killed. This -- this paragraph, therefore, is not correct; is that correct? Is that --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Let me answer. The situation as it was while I was there became even worse once I left. It is impossible that she died a natural death under such conditions. In any case, I accepted for the purposes of this Tribunal that she died of natural causes, and this is what I stand by.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, sir. So information you received subsequent to signing this statement that is before you now on the screen caused you to change your conclusions about the manner in which she died. You cannot exclude the possibility that these other individuals, likewise, had deaths that are different than the conclusions you draw for them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Sir, if you find the pieces of a body in a grave, isn't that a violent death? Or Hasna Alija and Hajra were found at the Jewish cemetery. They were mother and daughter. And you could clearly see they were -- they died a violent death. As for the Mutapcics, you could see on their bodies that they were killed by bullets. I attended the funerals of those people once their bodies had been exhumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would now like to move --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to be seeking to introduce the document. The testimony of the witness is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you now about some things that were unclear to me from your statement, which is P260 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We're returning to the statement today. And Your Honours and for the Prosecution, I do have a hard copy in B/C/S which might make it more easier for the witness to navigate through the same with the assistance of the usher. And after the opposing counsel has seen the same, I would ask that it be given to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we do that, I'm a bit confused by some of the answers which I would like to clarify. Mr. Crncalo, you were asked about the death of Ms. Ziba Kadic. You said the situation became worse after you left, and you say: "It is impossible that she died a natural death under such conditions." And then you said: "I accepted that for the purposes of this Tribunal that she died of natural causes." And you said that is what you stand by. That seems to be contradictory. Could you tell us now whether you accept for the possibility that she died from natural causes. Is that how I have to understand your testimony? Or do you still stand by that she died not from natural causes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for Ziba Kadic, I accepted that she died a natural death, and I still accept that. If it suffices, then, yes, I will gladly say that she died of natural causes. In any case, she did not live to see the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you say she died during the war, and you have no personal knowledge of how she died. Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no such knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just ask one further question on the questions that were asked by the Judge. Now, you have no personal knowledge that -- of how she died. You can therefore not say whether she was killed but neither can you say she died of natural causes, can you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say either. I have no proof either way. Since I can't prove she was killed, I will happily accept that she died of natural causes then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you can't accept that. Can you accept that, given the fact that you don't have the facts of how she died?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to accept that. I don't want to raise any doubts here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to ask you about paragraph 15 of your statement, P260.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is found in the B/C/S at page 5; on the English, at page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the question I want to ask you is, there you talk about the "situation returning to normal" until the end of 1991. Now since we have some paragraphs redacted from your statement, we do not have the full picture of what are you talking, so let me address that with you first. Am I correct that the, quote/unquote, situation you are referring to here at this paragraph was actually relating to the 6 May 1991 celebration of St. Georges Day by Mr. Vojislav Seselj and members of his party on the Romanija mountain?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is it also correct that at that time, when Mr. Seselj held this St. George Day celebration at Novakova Pecina, I believe, on the Romanija mountain, you personally saw this as a threat to the Muslim community of Pale?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: We had to see it that way. He went there to re-establish his Chetnik movement there. We had to be fearful.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Isn't it true, sir, that Novakova Pecina on the Romanija mountain is actually a historical landmark of the Hajduks' and later of the partizan anti-fascist struggle of all Yugoslavs and had nothing to do with the -- Mr. Seselj and his people known as Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Historically speaking, the Novakova Pecina location is such. Chetniks, however, did take shelter there, whereas the partisans never did. They were never there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I also correct that your primary concern at that time was that you were concerned that the Chetniks would drink alcohol during their gatherings and "then turn their anger towards our Muslim community."

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: The consumption of alcohol by the people we are now referring to as Chetniks was normal, regular. They didn't do much otherwise. A person under influence has no firm control over any actions, and of course we were concerned as to what would happen with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And arising out of your concerns, sir, am I correct that in May of 1991 you and other Muslims from your neighbourhood organised and participated in a guard watch?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: This is how it was. That same night, Izet Smajic, my neighbour and I, turned our lights in front of the houses and were walking about. At 1.00, 1.30, or 2.00 in the morning, a police car pulled in. Hujido [phoen] Kadric was in the vehicle as well as the deputy chief of police, Milan Simovic. They were touring the area and when Simovic saw me, since we used to be schoolmates, he asked me what happened, and I told him I have no idea, Seselj went up to Mount Romanija. And he said that three municipalities were sleepless that night. Fear nothing. If there's anything, just give me a call. There's no need to be afraid. Go back to your house. I told him, Well, I can go back in but I can't sleep any longer. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And so we can clarify, sir: Mr. Simovic and Mr. Kadric were both members of the local police in Pale.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One was a Serb, one was an ethnic Muslim; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did you then abandon your guard watch and go inside your house, as advised by these -- by these policemen?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I don't know if you can call it guard watch. But, in any case, my neighbour and I were outside. They left. And we stayed outside. We didn't go back into our houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How many days did you stay outside on -- on this type of watch? Night watch or guard watch.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Until Seselj left. For about a week or ten days or so. I can't be more precise. In any case, that's when we stopped coming outside during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, sir, then that after Mr. Seselj's party left Pale, after St. Georges Day, that the situation that had caused this tension dissipated and was no longer in existence?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Of course, it was -- it became easier for all of us once he left.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct, sir, that nothing bad happened to any members of the Bosnian Muslim community arising out of this gathering and celebration for St. Georges Day; that is to say, nothing bad happened even after Seselj's meeting or rally?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Nothing bad happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that this St. George Day celebration was an annual celebration that occurred in the years prior to 1991, not only at this location but throughout the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: The religious holiday of St. Georges Day is a Serb holiday. There were many families celebrating it. Traditionally speaking, the 6th of May was the gathering of the Hajduks who were mostly in forests and caves where they found shelter. During the St. Georges Day that year, they visited in the Novakova Pecina location. Seselj burst in and organised something there. I don't know what exactly. I only know that we were fearful.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in each of those prior years where St. Georges Day on the 6th of May had been celebrated in Pale municipality, it had transpired without any negative incidents against the Muslim community; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Sir, it wasn't just St. Georges Day that was celebrated but many other religious holidays. Before the political parties were organised, people of different religions invited their friends to their religious holidays to celebrate the Bajram and Christmas and other holidays. The situation was quite a good one. Once the political parties took over, all of the things that we are discussing now and all of the things because of which I am here now started happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, is there any recording of what was said by Mr. Seselj at that occasion so that we're better able to understand whether the witness was oversensitive or whether your questions are -- are suggesting something which is not realistic? Is there any recording of that? So that the Chamber might call that as evidence so as to better understand the evidence of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: None was identified to us, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's a public exhibit in another case at the Tribunal which is a recording of a speech Mr. Seselj gave around that time. We can review that and update the Chamber and Defence further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And perhaps I'm not -- we might be interested in any video of that, but we might also, first of all, be interested in a transcript of what he said, if that exists, so as to better be able to understand and evaluate the evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, after this celebration on the 6th of May, 1992, Mr. Seselj and his Chetniks, as you called them, that is to say, members of his radical party, they did not hold any rallies in Pale for the remainder of 1991 or 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Rallies in Pale started taking place in 1991, as far as I recall. This is the first time I get a question of that sort. It was around midsummer and late June or in July. That's when the rallies started taking place. There was a crisis in Kosovo and people were saying we won't give up Kosovo while carrying bottles of brandy in their hand. One couldn't say whether they were radicals or not because mostly civilians chanted such slogans.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I would like to refresh your recollection, so we have a clear and full answer, with the testimony that you gave in the Krajisnik case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This is -- this is document 1D291. It is page 82 in e-court. And while we wait for that, this is transcript page 5369, lines 4 through 14, of the witness's testimony in those proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, I will read for you, since there is no B/C/S translation of the -- of this transcript. The question that was posed, and it -- beginning like this: "Q. Try to be specific here, Mr. Crncalo. Forget the 6th of May. Let's move on from the 6th of May. When do you say that the next meeting after the 6th of May of the Chetniks was held? "A. I don't know. "Q. And, in fact, you don't know if any further meeting was held, do you? "A. Between the 6th of May and the next year 6th of May, I don't know whether there were any meetings of the Radical Party and these radical people. "Q. And when you say the Radical Party, you mean Chetniks, do you? "A. Yes." Sir, does this selection from your testimony in the Krajisnik proceedings comport to your recollections of the state of affairs following the 6th of May, 1991.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I remember clearly what things were like in the course of those days. As for the people shouting slogans about Kosovo, there were no symbols to be seen in -- so that one could say whether they were radicals or not, but there were columns marching down the street shouting, We will defend Serbhood. We won't give up Kosovo. That's how things were.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Before we get to -- well, let's -- let's -- before we get to Kosovo, do you stand by your testimony in the Krajisnik case, which I have just read to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your question suggests a contradiction between the two. So do you stand by this or do you stand by that. There is no such contradiction in the wordings I just had. So therefore, I think it might confuse the witness if you make him -- although you did not literally do that, but you make him choose between the two, and I think his last answer explained that already. Would you please be very precise and be fair to the witness in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will. I'm satisfied with the way it's in the transcript that he has explained. I will move on now to the second item he identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, you talked about a gathering relating to Kosovo and the conflict in Kosovo. Am I correct this was a one-time event that occurred in 1991 in Pale?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I still went to work in the engines factory Famos near Koran, and I could see then that there were columns being formed twice or three times per week. And the whole half of that year, things developed that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that you were present for the rally or that others told you what transpired at the rally?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Pale is a small place. Along the route from my house to the factory, that's where columns were formed and I passed by them. As for my attendance, what would I do there?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. If we can move on to a related topic. In paragraph 18 of your statement, that's P260, page 4 in the English, page 6 in the B/C/S, you again are talking about 1991 and how these Chetnik members did not physically mistreat you but you were affected psychologically. And you talk in your statement about how Serb Chetniks were a paramilitary group with a distinct uniform. And, sir, I put it to you that the only Chetniks in uniform that you ever saw in Pale municipality with your own eyes are just the two individuals that you saw at the petrol station who wore homemade uniforms and who are referenced in your statement. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: My statement is accurate. I stand by it. At the time, we all put such people wearing arms under one hat. As for the people you're referring to at the gas station, I could only identify them by their fur caps.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the men at the gas station that you referred to as Chetniks did not have arms; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: They did not have any weapons at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And those are the only two people you saw in Pale who you visually could identify as being Chetniks that caused all this tension for you.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: It's not because of them that this tension arose. It arose because of constant shooting from automatic weapons on the periphery of Pale. It never stopped, every night. That's what put fear into us. Hand-grenades were thrown on to the house of Bekir Jasarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, we're talking about 1991.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I still seek that we receive an answer. You told about the two people at the gas station. Did you, around that same time, see people dressed in a similar way apart from these two at a gas station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there were some not wearing a full uniform, but there were some who were wearing parts of a uniform, the upper part or the lower part. But I only saw those two wearing the fur hat and the -- the -- the sign of the -- skull and bones. I didn't see it on anyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These two were the only ones you saw wearing those hats and those skull-and-bones sign?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At paragraph 17 of your statement, you discuss the shooting of weapons in the air for Orthodox Christmas and other holidays. Am I correct that this is a tradition that took place every year prior to 1991 as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you use the word "for," whereas I read in the statement "after."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Let me rephrase the question. Perhaps I should cite the -- the -- the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, at paragraph 17, you say: "I know this because from time to time, especially after Orthodox Christmas and other Serb holidays, the Serbs would shoot those [sic] weapons in the air. I could hear the sound of the gun-fire and I could distinguish the sound from the shooting of hunting-type weapons." And my question for you, sir: Isn't it correct that this situation, the shooting of weapons after Christmas and other Serb holidays, was an annual occurrence that occurred in all the years prior to 1991 as well?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Mr. Lawyer, sir, I was born in Pale, and I know very well my Serb neighbours, and they know me and other Muslims. Nobody would ever mind if there was a wedding party or Christmas or any holiday, not only the new year, if somebody was firing a weapon. Nobody would mind or tell anyone anything. But when the shooting goes on every night, then something is wrong. Then there is an amount of fear and pressure created among the non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, show me in paragraph 17 where you say the shooting was every night? I read it as saying "time to time." Please clarify this statement that you have now made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, there's no use of asking the witness about every night. He said that from time to time, especially after, now that does not in any way contradict. And the witness, if he now clarifies it, he is fully entitled to do that, and then there's no use in asking him to point at paragraph 17 where, of course, we all can see it doesn't use the same language.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And he has testified that this truthful and accurate, he's reviewed it three times in three prior trials, and now he's got something different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, what is -- it's different language. Whether it's different from content, that is still to be seen. But, of course, you may further explore that matter and further ask for it. By the way, I notice that I understand paragraph 16 and 17 - and so do my colleagues - as primarily pointing at the type of weapons. Not primarily about that they were fired, for example, which may well be a custom on these holiday, although the witness also extends this too. But the type of weapon seems to be a very important part of this -- part of the statement. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to correct an inadvertent misstatement on the record. At page 42 of today's temporary transcript, line 16, Mr. Ivetic said Mr. Crncalo had verified the statement in three prior trials. The statement actually post dates his Krajisnik testimony and was not used in Stanisic and Zupljanin, so it's only one prior trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, having listened to all this, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I want to look at paragraph 16 of your statement, which was mentioned by Presiding Judge. That's page 3 in the English and page -- breaks over pages 5 and 6 in the B/C/S. In this paragraph, you talk about the Chetniks being armed and you talk about 50, possibly more, Chetniks that went to fight in Pakrac, Croatia, and kept their weapons. I would like to have you comment upon your testimony from the Krajisnik proceedings so we can better understand what this paragraph means.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would call up 1D291, pages 85 is the -- is the e-court reference. Although the section that I have will continue through page 87 of the transcript. And I'll wait for that and then I will begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It starts in the middle of the page at line 14, sir, and I will again read the English so that can you get the translation of the transcript. "Q. Is this -- this figure of 50 or about 50 that you put forward, is that based on what you were told by other people or heard from other people? "A. Well, when I was in the company of people, of those people, coming back from those battle-fields, when they were talking amongst themselves that they were in these [sic] two parts of the battle ground, listening to them, that's what I concluded. I didn't hear it from them, but listening to them talk, that's what I concluded. "Q. Were they people at work or people that you met in a cafe or what? "A. At work, and I don't frequent cafes much. So at work. "Q. So people from your work, is this what you say, people from your work went to fight in Croatia and returned from fighting in Croatia? Is that right? "A. Yes. "Q. In that case, presumably, Mr. Crncalo, if it's people from your work, you do have a pretty firm idea of how many were involved, don't you? "A. Where I work [sic] in the factory, there were 3.000 people, and I can't know each of those employees, all those workers. "Q. At that moment, I'm suggesting to you that even among 3.000 employees, you would have had a pretty firm idea of how many of those 3.000 went to Croatia and returned from fighting in Croatia. Is that not right? "A. Well, I didn't have a precise picture of it all, but that [sic] what was common knowledge, at least on the shift I was working, and we worked in three shifts. In the other two shifts, there were quite a number of people whom I didn't know, so I don't know whether they went or not. But the people working in my ... shift, they would say, and judging on what the other -- the men in the other ... shifts say -- but, as I say, I didn't know anybody personally, so I can't say. "Q. How many men were on your shift? "A. About 90. "Q. And how many -- was it the same people constantly, was it, broadly speaking, the same 90, not every day, but roughly speaking, it was the same group of men continuing on the same shift, month in, month out, was it? "A. Yes, mostly. But you know how it was. There would be new workers coming in. Some would retire, other young workers would come in. "Q. Yes, of course, there would be changes. That [sic] understood. How many men from your shift went to fight in Croatia? "A. Three." Sir, does this testimony from -- of yours from the Krajisnik proceedings comport to your recollection of how many men you had actual knowledge of that went to Pakrac, Croatia, from Pale municipality in 1991.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Those people coming back from Pakrac, sometimes during chance meetings I overheard what they were saying. They mentioned those two that you just referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I think that what -- what you are trying to establish is that the number the witness used for the 50 people returning from Pakrac is based on not direct observation by himself but on the basis of hearsay and that, therefore, the number of 50 people might not be as precise as suggested in the statement. Is that what you want to establish?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, I believe three is the part that he knows by hearsay. He does not know beyond three per the testimony in Krajisnik, as I read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure that accurately characterises the Krajisnik testimony. And the witness actually explains the number 50 two pages later in the same testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- okay. Let's try to see. Mr. Crncalo, in your statement, we find a number of 50 people returning from Pakrac. Have we well understood that -- that this was not personal knowledge of all these persons but that you concluded that approximately that number of people must have returned from Pakrac because that was what discussed at your workplace and which was, as you say in the statement, public secret. So not direct observation. Indirect observation. Perhaps the number not being very precise. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. You are quite right. Instead of 50, there may have been 150 who went from our municipality. But I heard about 50 from those people who returned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You also could not exclude that there were only 20 or 30?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One has to be realistic. I am not a military man inducting young recruits, giving them uniforms, sending them to Pakrac or elsewhere. I couldn't know these individuals, and I couldn't know the names of each person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, any matter you think is worthwhile to further elicit, you may do that in re-examination. Mr. Ivetic, I take it that your point has been addressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It has, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed. But also, think about the break in the next couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to finish at least this section so we have at least some continuity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With regard to these three people from work that went to Pakrac, am I correct that they were mobilised and they responded to mobilisation orders rather than volunteering?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: They were organised, mobilised, and they had received call-up papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And at that time, wasn't it the legal duty of every citizen of Yugoslavia that received call-up papers to respond and be mobilised by the army?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: You asked that question right. Until then, there was a law prevailing in the whole territory of Yugoslavia that all able-bodied men were obligated to report to the military department when called up. However, during those days that we are talking about, none of the Muslims were called up, only the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For the time being we are talking about these three Serb colleagues from your work that went to Pakrac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, it seems that your question addresses the possible illegality of having been called up to go to Croatia and to fight. I do not find anything of the kind in the statement. And I wonder whether it's the Prosecution's position that it would be illegal at that time for Serbs to respond to call-ups and to join your unit and go wherever you were sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I would first like to receive a response from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's a rather complex question that I'd like to an opportunity to think before I make a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So there's now --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I don't like to speak about such things off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, then we have no answer to that. Mr. Ivetic, you wanted to make an observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I was going to present the witness's sworn testimony where he indicated differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then -- yes, but the Chamber, of course, is not aware [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- was totally lost as far as the relevance of all that is concerned. Apart from that, of course, it's a question about legality, illegality, which requires a legal opinion rather than factual observation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think we can get this done in two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to direct your attention to page 88 of your testimony from Krajisnik which is transcript page 5375, lines 1 through 14, of 1D291, which is up on the screen. And here you are again talking about these three colleagues from work, and I will begin the quotation as follows: "Q. They weren't Chetniks, were they? "A. Well, I don't know what structures they were in. I really can't answer that. "Q. But was there anything about your three work colleagues to indicate that they were what you regarded as Chetniks? "A.
